name: Custom chin implant (silicone/Medpor)
summary: A solid or porous implant placed over the chin bone to add projection: the less invasive alternative to a sliding genioplasty, with its own trade-offs.
lead: A chin implant is an alloplastic (synthetic) device placed over the lower border of the mandible to increase the projection, and sometimes the height or width, of the chin. Common materials are silicone, porous high-density polyethylene (often sold as Medpor), expanded polytetrafluoroethylene and, more recently, patient-specific implants made from materials such as PEEK.
claims: An implant is a cheaper, easier alternative to genioplasty
A chin implant alone can fix a recessed profile
Custom implants give better results than stock implants
Implants can be removed later if unwanted

name: Chin filler
summary: Injectable filler (usually hyaluronic acid) placed at the chin to add projection or length without surgery; temporary, with rare but serious vascular complications.
lead: Chin filler is a non-surgical cosmetic treatment in which an injectable gel, typically hyaluronic acid, is placed in the chin to increase its projection, height or contour. It is sometimes called a liquid genioplasty and is used both for age-related volume loss and for congenital chin retrusion.
claims: Chin filler can approximate the look of surgery without surgery
The chin is a safe area to inject
Self-injected chin filler gives results comparable to a clinic

name: Vertical chin lengthening
summary: Genioplasty (or a graft or implant) that makes the chin taller rather than just more forward; documented in the surgical literature, mostly as small case series.
lead: Vertical chin lengthening refers to surgical techniques that increase the vertical height of the chin, as distinct from advancing it forward. Methods described in the literature include osseous genioplasty with interpositional bone grafts, pedicled grafts, and alloplastic materials.

name: Chin reduction / shaving
summary: Surgery to shrink a large chin by burring the bone or moving it back and up; documented in surgical papers, with nerve and contour risks.
lead: Chin reduction refers to surgical procedures that reduce the size of the chin in projection, height or width. A 1999 paper states that, at that time, surgical reduction of an isolated large chin was not a simple procedure, and that two operations existed: osteotomy with setback, or reduction of the prominence by burring.

name: Double-jaw surgery for retrognathia
summary: Bimaxillary (upper and lower jaw) surgery that moves a recessed mandible forward, often with the maxilla and chin; a major established operation with documented joint and nerve risks.
lead: Double-jaw surgery, or bimaxillary surgery, is an orthognathic operation in which both the maxilla (upper jaw) and the mandible (lower jaw) are cut, repositioned and fixed. For retrognathia, a recessed lower jaw, the mandible is advanced, commonly through a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, and the upper jaw is moved to match the bite.
claims: Single-jaw surgery plus genioplasty can match double-jaw results
Retrognathia is a diagnosable skeletal deformity that can be treated surgically

name: Profile analysis (Ricketts E-line)
summary: A line from nose tip to chin used to judge how far the lips sit from the profile; a standard orthodontic reference, with preferences that vary by observer.
lead: The E-line, or esthetic plane, is a soft-tissue reference line defined in Ricketts cephalometric analysis as running from the tip of the soft-tissue nose to the soft-tissue pogonion. It is used to describe the position of the lips relative to the nose and chin, with the lower lip to E-line distance (Li-EL) as a standard measurement.

name: Orthodontic functional appliances (Herbst, Twin Block)
summary: Orthodontist-fitted jaw-advancing braces for growing teens with an overbite; studied in randomized trials, but how much is real jaw growth versus tooth movement is debated.
lead: Orthodontic functional appliances are devices that hold or guide the lower jaw forward in growing children and adolescents, mainly to treat Class II malocclusion, in which the lower jaw sits behind the upper one and the upper front teeth overlap the lower ones. The best-known examples are the Herbst appliance, a fixed device with telescoping arms bonded to the teeth, and the Twin Block, a removable pair of acrylic bite plates .
claims: A Herbst appliance can lengthen a short lower jaw and fix a 'recessed' look.
Herbst appliances and elastics stunt upper-jaw (maxillary) growth.
Cheap mouth guards or home-made devices can substitute for a Herbst.
Functional appliances can improve the lower third of the face in people who are no longer growing.

name: Neck posture / forward head correction
summary: Pulling the head back over the shoulders to sharpen the profile; heavily studied for neck pain, but nobody has tested whether it changes how the chin looks.
lead: Forward head posture (FHP), sometimes called 'text neck' or 'nerd neck', is a posture in which the head sits forward of the shoulders, so the ear falls in front of a vertical line through the shoulder and the chin appears to poke forward . It is usually assessed clinically with the craniovertebral angle, formed between a horizontal line at the seventh cervical vertebra and a line to the ear .
claims: Correcting forward head posture improves the look of the jawline and profile.
Fixing forward head posture can make a recessed chin look worse.
Forward head posture in the teen years can affect upper-jaw (maxillary) growth.
Forward head posture causes pain and other problems throughout the body.

name: Jaw advancement for sleep apnea (MAD devices)
summary: A sleep-apnea mouthpiece that pushes the lower jaw forward; well studied for breathing, with no evidence it changes your face.
lead: A mandibular advancement device (MAD), also called a mandibular advancement splint or oral appliance, is a mouthpiece worn during sleep that holds the lower jaw slightly forward. It is used to treat snoring and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a condition of repeated airway collapse during sleep .

name: Fat grafting to chin
summary: Using your own fat to build out the chin; a recognized surgical technique in general, but the sources show little chin-specific evidence and the fat can partly resorb.
lead: Fat grafting, also called fat transfer or lipofilling, moves a person's own fat from one body area to another. It involves harvesting fat, processing it and reinjecting it, and is used to add volume or smooth irregular areas . Applied to the chin, it is one of several ways to change chin projection or contour, alongside implants, sliding genioplasty and injectable fillers .

name: Weight loss for chin definition
summary: Losing body fat to reveal the chin and jawline; plausible where fullness is soft tissue, but no studies test it and bone structure is not changed.
lead: Weight loss for chin definition refers to the idea that reducing body fat makes the chin and jawline look sharper by reducing fullness under the chin, often called a double chin. Wikipedia distinguishes two causes of a double-chin appearance: in some overweight people, subcutaneous fat around the neck creates a fold, while in others, often of normal weight, the jaw bones do not project far enough forward .

name: Submalar filler
summary: Filler injected below the cheekbone to add lower-midface volume; temporary, with only small registered trials in the sources reviewed.
lead: Submalar filler is an injectable filler placed in the hollow below the cheekbone to add volume to the lower midface. It is a non-surgical counterpart to submalar implants, which Wikipedia describes as augmenting the midface, while malar implants sit on the cheekbones .

name: Malar augmentation with fat grafting
summary: Your own liposuctioned fat injected into the cheeks for volume; plausible and widely used in the face, but cheek-specific evidence is thin.
lead: Malar augmentation with fat grafting is a cosmetic procedure in which a person's own fat is harvested, usually by liposuction from another body site, processed, and injected into the cheek area to add volume and projection over the cheekbones. It is a form of autologous (self-derived) soft-tissue augmentation, distinct from cheek implants and from hyaluronic acid fillers.

name: Zygomatic arch reduction / reduction malarplasty
summary: Cheekbone-narrowing osteotomy, mainly an East Asian aesthetic surgery, supported only by surgeon case series.
lead: Reduction malarplasty is a facial-bone surgery that narrows a wide or prominent cheekbone (zygoma) by cutting and repositioning the malar complex or zygomatic arch. Published authors describe it as one of the more commonly requested facial-contour procedures in East Asia and as rarely performed in the West.
claims: Flat cheekbones are really a recessed maxilla problem rather than a cheek problem

name: Cheekbone makeup contour/highlight
summary: Shading and highlighting to imitate defined cheekbones; reversible and low-risk, with no clinical research behind it.
lead: Cheekbone contouring and highlighting is a makeup technique in which darker shades are applied beneath the cheekbone and lighter or shimmering shades on top, intended to create the visual impression of more defined or higher cheekbones through shading.

name: Midface lift
summary: Surgery that lifts sagging cheek tissue; established in facial plastic surgery but backed mostly by surgeon case series.
lead: A midface lift is a cosmetic surgical procedure that repositions sagging cheek and lower-eyelid tissue upward, aiming to restore a fuller, younger-looking cheek and reduce the appearance of a hollowed lower lid. It is typically described as suited to patients in their 40s without marked jowling, and it can be combined with eyelid surgery.

name: Maxilla expansion for forward growth (face pulling/reverse-pull headgear)
summary: Orthodontic facemask that pulls a child's upper jaw forward; studied in kids with underbites, not an adult appearance tool.
lead: Reverse-pull headgear, also called a facemask or protraction facemask, is an orthodontic appliance with a frame in front of the face resting on the forehead and chin, with elastics attached to the teeth to pull the upper jaw forward. It is used in children with Class III malocclusion and a retrusive maxilla, often together with rapid palatal expansion.

name: Facial thread lift (cheek lifting)
summary: Threads placed under the skin to hoist the cheeks; minimally invasive, with unclear efficacy data and reported complications.
lead: A thread lift is a non-surgical or minimally invasive procedure in which threads, some with barbs or cones, are placed under the skin to lift facial tissue without removing skin. Applied to the cheeks, it is used to raise the midface and soften the nasolabial fold.

name: Cheek fat pad (Bichat) removal
summary: Surgical removal of the cheek fat pad for slimmer, hollower cheeks; popular online, with little published outcome data and nerve and duct risks.
lead: Cheek fat pad (Bichat) removal, also called buccal fat removal or bichectomy, is a surgical procedure in which part or all of the buccal fat pad, an encapsulated mass of fat deep in the cheek, is taken out, usually through the mouth, to reduce fullness of the lower cheek . In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a route to hollow cheeks and a more visible cheekbone-to-jaw transition, often alongside the idea of the ogee curve.
claims: Removing the buccal fat pad creates hollow cheeks and a better ogee curve.
Doing it yourself is a feasible alternative to surgery.

name: Hollow cheeks via chewing then fat loss
summary: Chew for the masseter, lean out for the cheeks; popular in forums, but no studies test the combination.
lead: "Hollow cheeks via chewing then fat loss" refers to a looksmaxxing approach that combines masseter-focused chewing with reducing body and facial fat, in order to show cheekbone and jaw structure. Proponents describe hollow cheeks as the shadowed area below the cheekbones, produced by bone, muscle and the amount of soft tissue .
claims: Hollow cheeks come from bone and masseter structure, with fat loss revealing them.
Overly hollow cheeks can look gaunt, and a thin fat layer may be preferable.

name: Frontal-orbital advancement (frontal bossing / brow)
summary: A forward brow and forehead goal in looksmaxxing; the surgical literature found covers brow lifts and brow reduction, not cosmetic advancement.
lead: In looksmaxxing usage, frontal-orbital advancement and frontal bossing refer to surgery or other changes meant to push the brow ridge and upper orbital area forward, producing a more prominent forehead and brow. The sources reviewed contain little direct material on this exact aim.

name: Ogee curve analysis
summary: The S-shaped line from cheekbone to cheek hollow, used as a goal in filler surgery and as a hotly promoted beauty marker online.
lead: In aesthetic facial surgery, the ogee curve describes the S-shaped line running from the cheekbone (malar prominence) down into the mid-cheek hollow . The word comes from geometry, where an ogee is an S-shaped curve joining a concave arc to a convex arc, and it is also used in architecture and engineering .
claims: A clear ogee curve separates a "chad" from a "normie".

name: Canthopexy
summary: Lower-lid tendon tightening without cutting the corner; well-established in blepharoplasty, unproven as an eye-shape tool.
lead: Canthopexy is a surgical procedure that tightens or repositions the lower eyelid by anchoring the lateral canthal tendon, without cutting the eyelid margin at the outer corner. Surgical papers present it as a routine companion to lower blepharoplasty that restores lid tone and contour and reduces the chance of lower lid malposition .
claims: Canthopexy gives a better almond or fox eye than canthoplasty.
Canthopexy results relax back within a year or two.

name: Tarsal strip procedure
summary: A surgical lower-lid tightening technique from eyelid medicine that forum users discuss for sagging lids and scleral show; evidence is mostly functional, not cosmetic.
lead: The tarsal strip procedure, or lateral tarsal strip, is an oculoplastic operation that tightens a lax lower eyelid by anchoring the outer end of the lid to the lateral orbital rim. It was published in 1979 as a technique for paralytic or senile upper and lower lid laxity, lateral canthal tendon laxity or malposition, and for scarring-related lid shortening problems after earlier lid-tightening surgery.

name: Medial epicanthoplasty
summary: Surgery that releases or removes the inner-corner eyelid fold to open the eye; well described in the Asian blepharoplasty literature, mostly as case series.
lead: Medial epicanthoplasty is a cosmetic and reconstructive operation that reduces or removes the epicanthal fold, a vertical skin fold that partially covers the inner corner of the eye. The fold is particularly common in East Asian populations, where the epicanthal fold is described as frequently coexisting with a missing upper eyelid crease.
claims: Epicanthoplasty can correct a narrow-looking eye spacing caused by 'mongolic folds'.
Post-surgical marks can be hidden with makeup within a few weeks.

name: Double eyelid surgery (Asian blepharoplasty)
summary: Surgery that creates an upper-lid crease; one of the most commonly performed cosmetic procedures in East Asia, with a large surgical literature but few controlled trials.
lead: Double eyelid surgery, also called Asian blepharoplasty or supratarsal fold creation, is an operation that forms a crease in the upper eyelid. Surgical authors note that Asian upper lids often have no superior palpebral fold, along with excess fat, pretarsal skin laxity and a medial epicanthal fold.

name: Non-incisional double eyelid (suture method)
summary: Buried-suture double eyelid surgery creates a crease with stitches instead of an incision; popular in Asia, with literature focused on crease loss and suture complications.
lead: Non-incisional (buried suture) double eyelid surgery creates an upper-lid crease by placing stitches through the lid rather than cutting skin. Surgical papers describe it as one of two alternative approaches, the other being the incision method, and as very popular in Asia, especially China.

name: Ptosis surgery (levator advancement)
summary: Surgery to raise a drooping upper lid, mainly a functional operation whose appearance benefit (a more open eye) is discussed on forums; supported in medical series.
lead: Ptosis surgery corrects drooping of the upper eyelid (blepharoptosis). Levator advancement, also called aponeurotic ptosis surgery, repairs the levator aponeurosis that has stretched or detached from the tarsal plate, and was described in the ophthalmic literature in 1979 with emphasis on preserving normal anatomy.
claims: Ptosis repair gives a more open, more attractive eye.

name: Oxymetazoline eye drops (Upneeq)
summary: A prescription 0.1% oxymetazoline eye drop approved for acquired ptosis that lifts the lid slightly; forum users discuss cheaper nasal-spray substitutes, which are not the approved product.
lead: Upneeq is a brand of 0.1% oxymetazoline hydrochloride ophthalmic solution, approved by the US FDA in July 2020 to treat acquired blepharoptosis (drooping of the upper eyelid). Oxymetazoline is an imidazole-derivative alpha-adrenergic agonist developed from xylometazoline at Merck in 1961, and is also used in nasal sprays, redness drops and a rosacea cream.
claims: A nasal spray can be used as an alternative to Upneeq eye drops.

name: Eyelid tape / fold stickers
summary: Thin adhesive strips that press the upper lid into a temporary crease; a cosmetic stopgap with a small but real research literature on ocular effects.
lead: Eyelid tape, also sold as fold stickers or double eyelid tape, consists of thin adhesive strips applied to the upper eyelid to create a temporary crease. Many East Asians use the product to produce a double eyelid effect as a temporary means of increasing perceived beauty . It is the non-surgical counterpart to double eyelid surgery, which creates a permanent crease in people who do not have one naturally .
claims: Eyelid tape can fake a double eyelid or open a hooded eye
Eye drops plus eye rolling can fix ptosis
Daily tape use is harmless
